title: Chapter 66 — The Shark Massacre
paragraphs: When in the Southern Fishery a captured Sperm Whale, after long and weary toil, is brought alongside late at night, it is not, as a general rule, customary to proceed at once with cutting him in. For that business is an extremely laborious one, is not soon completed, and requires all hands. Therefore, the common usage is to take in sail, haul back the mainyard, and let the ship drift alongside her prize through the night, leaving everything to be dealt with in the morning.

But sometimes, especially near the Line in the Pacific, this plan will not work at all, because such incalculable hosts of sharks gather around the moored carcass that if it were left so for six hours, say, little more than the skeleton would remain by morning. In most other parts of the ocean, however, where these fish do not so largely abound, the usual practice may be followed without much risk.

Nevertheless, upon Stubb setting the anchor-watch after his supper was finished, and when Queequeg and a forecastle seaman came on deck, no small excitement was created among the sharks. For immediately hanging the cutting stages over the side and lowering three lanterns to cast long gleams of light over the murky sea, these two men began cutting the dead whale with their sharp whaling-spades. Queequeg wielded his blade with the skill and vigor that would have done credit to the most experienced surgeon. And Queequeg's keen spade, meanwhile, sliced deep into the thick hide, sending broad swaths of blubber flying over the side. But the fiends below were not content to wait. They kept biting at the blubber that hung from the whale, and sometimes even at the spade itself.

The whaling-spade used for cutting-in is made of the very best steel, about the size of a man's spread hand. In general shape it resembles the garden tool after which it is named, only its sides are perfectly flat and its upper end considerably narrower than the lower. This weapon is always kept as sharp as possible. And when being used, is occasionally whetted, just as a razor is stropped. Sometimes a very practiced hand will keep the blade sharp enough to shave off the thin surface of the body without drawing blood.
"Queequeg no care what god made him shark," said the harpooner, agonizingly lifting his hand up and down. "Whether Fiji god or Nantucket god — but the god that made shark must be one damn Indian."
